messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Firefighter
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Name Reminders: Hearing related names, Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Sleep: Going to sleep or lying in the dark, Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person

Vignette:
For much of his adult life, Minh had worked as a firefighter, a role that had trained him to move toward danger rather than away from it. Even now, at 77, he still spoke of himself as someone who had spent years responding to other people’s emergencies without hesitation. But in the period he spent as a civilian in a war zone, that familiar sense of competence and purpose had been overturned. He did not describe the event in grand terms; instead, he returned to a specific night marked by sirens, confusion, and the blunt force of an explosion that seemed to split the air around him. He had been in a setting where ambulance sounds carried a particular weight, and even now those sounds brought the whole scene back with unnerving force. He recalled hearing names shouted in the chaos and later finding that even hearing related names in ordinary conversation could tug him back toward that time, as if those syllables were a doorway he did not want opened.

Minh said the frightening event remained painfully clear in his mind, with sharp details he could not scrub away. At the same time, he experienced the memory as strangely separate from himself, as though it belonged to someone else’s life rather than his own. He could describe it vividly, but when it arrived uninvited, it did not feel like a recollection he chose to hold; it forced its way into his mind when he was trying to think of something else. He found that if he allowed himself to think about it directly, he became convinced he would not be able to handle what came up. That belief made him push the memory away whenever possible, although it still intruded, often without warning. He spoke about the event with a kind of distance, as if he were recounting a report rather than a personal history, and at times he said he felt like an object, not like a person, reduced to someone acted upon by forces beyond his control.

In the months and years that followed, certain moments in daily life became charged with the same fear. As a firefighter, ambulance calls and emergency scenes remained part of the world around him, and he noticed how quickly his body would tense when he heard the sound of an ambulance approaching or saw one in traffic. He could be standing at the station or out with his wife and feel himself scanning automatically, searching for signs that something was about to happen. He was constantly checking the surroundings, eyes moving to doorways, vehicles, and people’s hands before he had fully registered doing it. Explosion sounds, or even a bang that might otherwise have seemed ordinary, could set off the same surge of alertness. At home, evenings became harder because he dreaded going to sleep and especially lying in the dark, when there was nothing to distract him from what might enter his mind. He would delay going to bed, stay up longer than he needed to, or keep a light on rather than settle into darkness.

Minh also noticed that when memories or reminders surfaced, his thoughts did not stay in the present for long. He found himself imagining revenge against the people he held responsible, and although he did not present these fantasies as plans, he described them as a way his mind returned again and again to the injustice of what had happened. Alongside this, there was a persistent sense that his own experience should somehow have been different. He believed somebody else would not have gotten into such a situation, and that comparison left him feeling singled out in a way that was humiliating as well as frightening. The feeling of being reduced to an object, rather than a person with choice or dignity, remained part of how he understood that period of his life. He did not say these thoughts had disappeared; rather, they sat with him in the background, especially when he was tired, alone, or exposed to reminders in the outside world.

By the time he came for help, Minh was living with his wife and trying to preserve his routines, but his world had narrowed around what he could tolerate. He had begun to organize evenings to avoid being in bed too early, and he remained wary of dark rooms and sudden noises. He could still function, but with a constant inward vigilance that left him exhausted. What finally brought him in was the accumulation of these moments: the jolt when an ambulance passed, the unease when someone said a name too close to the ones he remembered, the way a bang could send him back to that night before he had time to brace himself. He said he was most afraid that if he tried to think about it too much, it would overwhelm him, yet he was also hoping that speaking about it carefully might make it possible to sleep without dread and to feel, again, more like himself than like something that had simply been carried through the war.
